title: Bhṛgu asks his father: the mark of Brahman, and the way of austerity
theme: The third vallī opens with a story: a son asks his father to teach him Brahman, is given a list of doors and a definition — that from which beings are born, by which they live, into which they return — and is left to find it by austerity.

words.context: Kūranārāyaṇa identifies him with the Bhṛgu of the Gītā («इति प्रसिद्धो वारुणिः»)
Śaṅkara: the particle recalls something well known («प्रसिद्धानुस्मारकः»)
Govindarāja: the son does not look for another teacher while a father who knows Brahman is alive («पितरि ब्रह्मज्ञे विद्यमाने नान्यं ब्रह्मज्ञानाय उपसरेत्»)

words.role: object of provāca, explained by the list that follows

words.context: Śaṅkara: the breath within the body, the eater («तदभ्यन्तरं च प्राणम् अत्तारम्»)
Raṅgarāmānuja: the ablative of cause («अत्र यत इति पञ्चमी हेत्वार्थिका»)
written vā before imāni; Govindarāja reads the particle vai («वै इति योगिप्रसिद्धिः»)

words.role: verb of the first relative clause
verb of the second relative clause
first verb of the third clause
words.context: Bhāradvāja: at release, the beings go towards it («मोक्षकाले यद्वस्तु उद्दिश्य सर्वभूतानि प्रयन्ति»); Śaṅkara: at their destruction

words.role: second verb of the third clause
words.context: Śaṅkara: they become one with it («अभिसंविशन्ति तादात्म्यमेव प्रतिपद्यन्ते»)
Raṅgarāmānuja: the cause is restated and Brahmanhood is predicated of it («तद्ब्रह्मेति कारणस्य ब्रह्मत्वं विधीयते»)

words.role: prior action; the sentence is completed at the start of 3.2

sandhi.rule: The final s of bhṛgus becomes ru, P. 8.2.66 (ससजुषो रुँः), and appears as r before the voiced v.

sandhi.type: visarga before a voiced consonant; guṇa
sandhi.rule: bhagavaḥ before the voiced b: the visarga becomes u, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च), and a + u gives o, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः). brahma + iti → brahmeti, also by P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः).
ai before a vowel becomes āy, P. 6.1.78 (एचोऽयवायावः), and the y is dropped, P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य); the hiatus that results stays.

sandhi.type: visarga before a voiced consonant; ai before a vowel
sandhi.rule: yataḥ before v: P. 6.1.114 (हशि च) and P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः). vai before i: āy by P. 6.1.78 (एचोऽयवायावः), y dropped by P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य), so vai imāni is written vā imāni.
i before a dissimilar vowel becomes y: P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).
A final t becomes d before a voiced consonant: P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).

sandhi.type: saḥ before a consonant; aḥ before a
sandhi.rule: saḥ loses its ending before a consonant, P. 6.1.132 (एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि). tapaḥ before a: the visarga becomes u, P. 6.1.113 (अतो रोरप्लुतादप्लुते), a + u → o, and the following a is absorbed, P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति), written with avagraha.
The visarga becomes s before t: P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः).

morphology.note: A patronymic, ‘son of Varuṇa’, formed with the taddhita -i; Govindarāja cites P. 4.1.95 (अत इञ्) («वरुणस्य ऋषेः अपत्यं वारुणिः»).
The Vedic vocative of bhagavat (classical bhagavan): Govindarāja cites P. 8.3.1 (मतुवसो रु सम्बुद्धौ छन्दसि), by which the final of a stem in -vat becomes ru in the vocative in the Veda.
Perfect of upa-√sṛ, ‘go near’; used of a pupil approaching a teacher in due form.
Desiderative of vi-√jñā (‘wish to know distinctly’), imperative, ātmanepada; the desiderative of √jñā takes ātmanepada by P. 1.3.57 (ज्ञाश्रुस्मृदृशां सनः).
Imperfect of √tap in the middle (ātmanepada) with tapas as its object, ‘practised austerity’; P. 3.1.88 (तपस्तपःकर्मकस्यैव) gives √tap this construction only when its object is tapas.
The sentence is left open: ‘having practised austerity, …’; its main verb is vyajānāt at the start of 3.2. The same open ending closes 3.2–3.5.

translation.literal: Bhṛgu, indeed, Vāruṇi, approached [his] father Varuṇa: ‘Teach [me] Brahman, venerable one.’ To him he declared this: ‘food, breath, eye, ear, mind, speech.’ He said to him: ‘That from which, indeed, these beings are born; that by which, born, they live; that into which they go forth [and] enter — seek to know that. That is Brahman.’ He practised austerity. Having practised austerity —
translation.readable: Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa, went to his father Varuṇa and said, ‘Sir, teach me Brahman.’ Varuṇa named for him food, breath, sight, hearing, mind and speech, and then said: ‘That from which these beings are born, that by which they live once born, and that into which they pass and merge at the end — seek to know that. That is Brahman.’ Bhṛgu practised austerity, and when he had practised it —

syntax: A narrative frame in the perfect (upasasāra, provāca, uvāca) around two speeches. The first speech is a bare list in the accusative (annam … vācam iti), the object of provāca. The second is a single sentence with three relative clauses (yataḥ … jāyante; yena … jīvanti; yat prayanti abhisaṃviśanti), resumed by tat, the object of the imperative vijijñāsasva, and closed by a predication, tad brahma. The narrative resumes in the imperfect (atapyata) and breaks off on an absolutive (taptvā) whose main verb begins the next anuvāka.

ambiguities.note: The text is written yato vā imāni. Sandhi allows vā (‘or’) or vai (‘indeed’, ai becoming ā before a vowel). Govindarāja reads vai («वै इति योगिप्रसिद्धिः»); the padaccheda follows him, since ‘or’ gives no sense here. Śaṅkara and Bhāradvāja only repeat the words.

Śaṅkara: the list names the doors through which Brahman is apprehended, the body, breath and the organs («ब्रह्मोपलब्धौ द्वाराण्युक्तवान्»). Kūranārāyaṇa reads it as naming the twenty-four principles («एवं चतुर्विंशतितत्त्वसङ्ग्रहणम्»); Rāmānanda and Bhāradvāja take Varuṇa to be saying ‘food is Brahman, breath is Brahman’, which leaves the son confused and prompts the definition.

‘They go forth’: Śaṅkara takes it of death and dissolution, with abhisaṃviśanti as becoming one with Brahman. Raṅgarāmānuja and Bhāradvāja allow that prayanti may mean going to Brahman at release and abhisaṃviśanti dissolution at the end of a world-age.

Kūranārāyaṇa: it enjoins meditation («अतः तद्विजिज्ञासस्व उपासनं कुरु»). Raṅgarāmānuja: it enjoins neither inquiry nor meditation, but asks for attention to the definition being given («तद्विजिज्ञासस्व इति न विचारस्य उपासनस्य वा विधिः»).

metre.name: prose
metre.note: Prose (brāhmaṇa style) in short clauses, divided at the daṇḍas.

beginner: A young man named Bhṛgu goes to his father, the god Varuṇa, and asks, “Teach me what Brahman is.” His father does not give him a neat answer. First he names some things to look at: food, breath, the eye, the ear, the mind and speech. Then he gives him a test that anything claiming to be Brahman must pass: it must be the source from which all beings are born, the support by which they live, and the place into which they return at the end. “Find out what that is,” he says. Bhṛgu does not ask for more. He goes away and practises austerity — disciplined effort and focused reflection — to discover the answer for himself.
analogy: A teacher who gives a student the properties a solution must have, and then leaves the student to find it, teaches more than one who hands over the answer.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Bhṛgu, son of Varuṇa, approaches his father and asks to be taught Brahman. Varuṇa names food, breath, eye, ear, mind and speech, and then defines Brahman as that from which beings are born, by which they live and into which they return; he tells his son to seek to know it. Bhṛgu practises austerity.

commentary.q: Why does the third vallī begin with a story?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: the teaching of Brahman was completed in the second vallī («परिसमाप्ता च ब्रह्मविद्या । अतः परं ब्रह्मविद्यासाधनं तपो वक्तव्यम्»); what remains is the means, austerity, and the meditations on food and the rest. The story praises the knowledge, because a father taught it to his beloved son («आख्यायिका विद्यास्तुतये»). Rāmānanda says the same and adds that it is therefore not to be taught to the unfit («आख्यायिका विद्यास्तुतिद्योतनार्था»).

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: Brahman is that whose nature beings do not leave at their origin, life or dissolution — «उत्पत्तिस्थितिलयकालेषु यदात्मतां न जहति भूतानि, तदेतद्ब्रह्मणो लक्षणम्». Raṅgarāmānuja, Rāmānanda and Gopālānanda (modern) all insist that the three together are the definition, not each alone («अतः समुदितमेव लक्षणम्»; «समुदितमेव लक्षणं ब्रह्मणः न तु प्रत्येकम्»; «त्रितयं समुदितं लक्षणम्»): otherwise one might suppose a second cause of the world’s life or end. Raṅgarāmānuja adds that ‘from which, by which, into which’ restates a cause already known, and ‘that is Brahman’ predicates Brahmanhood of it («यतः येन यत् इति यद्वृत्तयोगात् कारणम् अनूद्यते । तद्ब्रह्मेति कारणस्य ब्रह्मत्वं विधीयते»).

commentary.q: Why does Varuṇa not simply say what Brahman is?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: Varuṇa left the teaching incomplete on purpose, since he did not name Brahman directly («साक्षाद्ब्रह्मणोऽनिर्देशात्»); from this Bhṛgu understood that another means was needed, and took up austerity, the most effective means of all. That austerity is the concentration of the outer and inner organs («तच्च तपो बाह्यान्तःकरणसमाधानम्»), and Śaṅkara supports it with a smṛti verse he cites: «मनसश्चेन्द्रियाणां च ह्यैकाग्र्यं परमं तपः».

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Govindarāja gives two readings: Bhṛgu performed fasts such as the cāndrāyaṇa, or he reflected («चान्द्रायणादिकम् अकरोत् । यद्वा आलोचनम् अकरोत्»), deriving tapas also from tap ‘to consider’. Bhāradvāja-Rāmānuja makes it the restraint of the senses («इन्द्रियनियमनलक्षणरूपं तपः»). Kūranārāyaṇa: once the thing to be known and its mark were taught, the pupil practised austerity to see it directly («एवं लक्ष्ये लक्षणे च उपदिष्टे शिष्यः स तपोऽतप्यत तत्साक्षात्कारार्थम्»).

commentary.q: What do the forms tell us?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Govindarāja: yataḥ is an ablative of cause, which shows Brahman to be both the efficient and the material cause («यतः इति हेतौ पञ्चमी । तेन अभिन्ननिमित्तोपादानसिद्धिः»); Raṅgarāmānuja too reads the ablative as causal. The vocative bhagavaḥ is a Vedic form (see morphology). The anuvāka ends on an absolutive, taptvā, so that the sentence runs on into the next.

advaita.text: The definition points to Brahman as that whose nature beings never leave at birth, life or death; the list names the doors through which it is approached. The third vallī adds nothing new to the knowledge, which is complete; it teaches its means, austerity, understood as concentration of mind and senses («तच्च तपो बाह्यान्तःकरणसमाधानम्»).

visistadvaita.text: Brahman is defined as the one cause, efficient and material, of the world’s origin, life and dissolution, the three taken together. Kūranārāyaṇa draws a further point from the words: because beings are said to be born and to perish, they are real — «जन्मविनाशादिवचनात् सत्यत्वमपि भूतानाम् उक्तम्» — for no one speaks of the birth and death of a snake that is only a garland seen wrongly («न हि मिथ्याभूतस्य स्रक्सर्पस्य तत्र जन्मविनाशौ»). Raṅgarāmānuja distinguishes two kinds of definition: causality marks Brahman as qualified by the world, while satyaṃ jñānam marks Brahman in itself («जगत्कारणत्वलक्षणं विशिष्टनिष्ठम्»; «सत्यज्ञानत्वलक्षणं तु विशेष्यनिष्ठम्»).

dvaita.text: Madhva has no separate comment on this anuvāka; his single comment on the following ones reads the list of 3.1 as names of Viṣṇu — he is ‘eye’ because he sees («चक्षुः स चष्टे यद् विष्णुः») — and austerity as contemplation of knowledge, by which Bhṛgu came to know Janārdana step by step («ज्ञानानुसन्धानरूपतपसा तं जनार्दनम्»).

schools.disagreement: All agree that Brahman is the cause of the world and that austerity is the means to know it. Śaṅkara reads the definition as pointing beyond the world to the Self whose nature beings never leave; Kūranārāyaṇa and Raṅgarāmānuja read it as establishing Brahman as the real cause of a real world, and Kūranārāyaṇa argues explicitly against the illusion reading; Madhva reads every name as a name of Viṣṇu. They also differ on the austerity: concentration (Śaṅkara), sense-restraint or fasting and reflection (Bhāradvāja, Govindarāja), contemplation of knowledge (Madhva).

parallels.note: The second sūtra of the Brahmasūtra defines Brahman as that from which the origin, maintenance and dissolution of this world proceed. Raṅgarāmānuja discusses this anuvāka with it; the sūtra is generally taken to rest on this sentence.
Śaṅkara cites this verse to show that breath, eye, ear and mind are doors to Brahman, ‘the breath of breath, the eye of the eye’.
The Muṇḍaka’s rule that one seeking knowledge should go to a teacher with fuel in hand; Govindarāja and Kūranārāyaṇa cite it for Bhṛgu’s approach.
Kūranārāyaṇa identifies the Bhṛgu of this story with the great seer named in the Gītā.

contemporary.text: Varuṇa could have given his son an answer. Instead he gives criteria and sends him away to work. Good mentors still do this: they say what a good solution must achieve, let the learner try candidates, and stay available when the learner comes back unsatisfied. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: When did someone help you most by not giving you the answer?
reflect.deeper: What would have to be true of something for it to be the source, the support and the end of everything? Can anything you know meet all three conditions?
reflect.practice: For a few minutes, sit still and let the senses quiet down, as the commentators describe austerity; notice what remains when the eye, ear and speech are at rest.

references.text: Madhva’s digital text does not print this anuvāka as mūla (logged in corrections.json as an omission of the witness); his one comment on 3.2–3.7 also explains the list given here.
The Kūranārāyaṇa file for this anuvāka begins with a long survey of the two earlier vallīs; it also carries an editor’s footnote quoting Śaṅkara, which is not quoted here as Kūranārāyaṇa’s.

flags.note: yato vā imāni: the padaccheda takes vai with Govindarāja; ‘or’ (vā) is grammatically possible but gives no sense.
Whether vijijñāsasva enjoins meditation (Kūranārāyaṇa) or only asks for attention (Raṅgarāmānuja).
